engineering.label: Engineering
engineering.title: The parts worth naming.
engineering.intro: Four decisions that cost time up front and are painful to retrofit later.

entries.title: Multi-tenant authorization, checked by a test that reads the source
entries.body: The tourist board and every business share one database, so a single leak ends the pilot. Permissions run through WorkOS FGA with a synchronous grant cache, and a source-level test fails the build on any route that reads data without checking.

entries.title: Retrieval that knows when to skip the vector index
entries.body: Opening hours go to a structured lookup, a menu photo to a multimodal index. Read from a column, an opening time is a fact. Guessed from a vector store, a wrong closing time is the thing a guest remembers.

entries.title: Scraping and pedestrian routing run as our own services
entries.body: Content ingestion and OSRM walking routes are self-hosted on Railway, not rented per request. Directions priced per request turn a busy August into a bill nobody forecast.

entries.title: A design system with its own test suite
entries.body: Sixteen governed subsystems make up the shared interface, tested like the rest of the code. A fix to one component reaches every surface in one change.

hero.name: Polis Interface
hero.claim: Civic infrastructure that treats government data as something you check, not something you believe.

stats.label: Services
stats.note: Four apps on top of them.

whatItIs.label: What it is
whatItIs.title: A governance graph, not a document dump
whatItIs.intro: Polis models what a public body actually produces — decisions, promises, budgets, meetings, officials — as a graph. Every public claim in that graph points back to the source document it came from, and the document carries proof of its own integrity.
whatItIs.surfacesBody: A campaigning surface publishes a program. An accountability layer tracks the same program against what was delivered. Both read the same verifiable records, so the promise page and the record page cannot drift apart while nobody is looking.
whatItIs.addressBody: "The council approved the budget in March" is not a sentence in Polis. It is an edge to a decision, which resolves to a filed document, which resolves to a hash, a seal, and a timestamp a stranger can re-check without asking anyone's permission.

engineering.label: Engineering
engineering.title: Where the trust actually comes from
engineering.intro: Four pieces are worth naming, because they are the parts a public buyer or an auditor would go looking for.

entries.title: The audit ledger is hash-chained inside the insert transaction
entries.body: Each event stores the hash of the event before it, computed and written in the same transaction that inserts the row. Two writers racing each other cannot both win.
entries.why: An audit log you can quietly reorder afterwards is not evidence of anything.

entries.title: Documents are verified, not just uploaded
entries.body: A canonical hash, an eIDAS-shaped e-seal, and an RFC 3161 timestamp from an outside authority travel with the file. Redaction rules take precedence over publication, so a document can be proved authentic without exposing what should stay closed.
entries.why: Authentic and publishable are two different questions. Systems that answer them together leak.

entries.title: Policy gates fail closed
entries.body: Ten OPA/Rego modules decide who may read and write what. When the policy layer cannot answer, the request is denied rather than allowed through.
entries.why: Most access-control bugs are a check that silently returned nothing and was read as a yes.

entries.title: An elected official cannot mark their own promise delivered
entries.body: The accountability layer keeps the actor who claims separate from the actor who confirms. A status change to delivered records who confirmed it, and that person is not the subject of the promise.
entries.why: Self-reported delivery is the standard failure mode of a promise tracker.

engineering.closing: eIDAS, RFC 3161, GDPR-shaped redaction: the regulation sits in the data model, not in a compliance appendix written after the build.

honesty.label: Honesty as a feature
honesty.title: The status label is part of the product
honesty.intro: Polis labels every surface in its own documentation as [verifiable], [demonstration/stub], or [not yet live]. The simulated pilot says it is simulated in its first line.
labels: Backed by data in the system. Follow it to a source document and check the hash yourself.
The screen works; what sits behind it is a placeholder. Do not plan a rollout around it.
honesty.closing: This is what an institution buying software should demand, screen by screen. A vendor who can tell you which of their screens is real, which is a demo, and which is a slide has given you something to plan against.

evidence.label: Evidence
evidence.title: How a document becomes checkable
evidence.intro: There are no screenshots on this page — Polis is not deployed, and a screenshot of an undeployed system proves nothing. This is the pipeline as built: from the file a clerk uploads to the verdict a citizen gets.

pipeline.title: Document trust pipeline
pipeline.subtitle: source file → public verdict

stages.name: Document
stages.detail: A decision, contract, or set of minutes, exactly as filed.

stages.name: Canonicalize
stages.detail: Bytes normalized to one form, then hashed. Same file, same hash, every time.

stages.name: Seal
stages.detail: The issuing body signs the hash, not the file. eIDAS-shaped e-seal.

stages.name: Timestamp
stages.detail: An RFC 3161 authority attests that the hash existed at a given moment.

stages.name: Registry
stages.detail: Hash, seal, and token are recorded together and linked to the claims that cite them.

stages.name: Verify
stages.detail: Anyone re-hashes the file and checks it against the record. No account needed.

pipeline.ledgerSubtitle: each row carries the row before it
ledgerRows: Minutes accepted; hash, seal, and timestamp written.
A program item is bound to the decision it depends on.
Status moves to delivered — recorded with the confirming actor, who is not the official.
pipeline.caption: Hashes here are illustrative. In the running code, a row's previous-hash is computed and written inside the same transaction that inserts the row, so two writers racing each other cannot end up with two valid chains.

next.title: Where a claim has to be checkable.
next.body: If you are building something where a citizen, an auditor, or a regulator has to be able to check the claim rather than take it on trust, that is the conversation we want.
next.noteP1: Polis is pre-deployment. No public body runs it. The pilot in the repository is simulated and labels itself simulated in its first line. External integrations — registries, timestamp authorities, identity providers — are stubbed behind interfaces.
next.noteP2: The code, the schema, the policy modules, and the tests are real and public. The deployment is not.

whatItDoes.label: What it does
whatItDoes.title: Funding you qualify for, before the deadline
whatItDoes.intro: EU funding is public money that is hard to find. Calls land on SEDIA and TED as long documents with their own vocabulary, eligibility rules and deadlines. Most organizations hear about the right one too late.
whatItDoes.body: Funda watches those sources on a schedule, turns each call into a structured record, and puts it in front of the organizations that match. Consultants work a portfolio of clients against the same feed. One dataset, read four ways.
whatItDoes.note: Funda is in active build. There is no public deployment, no customer data behind these screens, and no results to report yet. Every number on this page counts something that exists in the codebase today.

surfaces.note: The people who run the platform

surfaces.name: Corporate
surfaces.note: The organization applying for the funding

matching.label: How matching works
matching.title: From a published call to the right inbox

steps.name: Read the sources
steps.body: Agents pull calls from SEDIA and TED as they publish, instead of waiting for someone to check a portal.

steps.name: Turn documents into fields
steps.body: Each call becomes a record: who may apply, for what, in which regions, by when.

steps.name: Score against the organization
steps.body: An organization's profile is compared field by field — sector, size, and where it actually operates, which is where the geospatial part earns its keep.

steps.name: Route it to a person
steps.body: Matches land on the surface that role uses, in that user's language.

shows.label: What it shows
shows.title: Same shape, smaller footprint
shows.p1: Voyager is where we built retrieval that stays grounded in a client's own content. On Polis, the hard part was an audit trail that makes a claim checkable. Funda carries both at a smaller scale: ingestion that has to be accurate, matching a user can argue with, and four roles reading one typed dataset.
shows.p2: The stack is deliberately small — Next.js on the front, Convex for data and functions, Clerk for identity and roles. The hard part is keeping an agent pipeline honest when the input is a call document written in institutional language and the output is a decision someone will act on.

next.title: Have a system with this shape?
next.body: Tell us what it has to read, who has to see the result, and what happens if it is wrong. We will tell you what it takes.

pipeline.label: How we ship these
pipeline.title: Instagram profile in, live URL out
pipeline.intro: The same six steps every time, run as one continuous pass. That is why the date we give you holds.

steps.name: Read the Instagram profile
steps.body: We start from what the business already publishes — posts, captions, photos, opening hours. Nobody has to write a brief.

steps.name: Pull the content apart
steps.body: Services, prices, location and tone of voice come out of that material and get sorted into the pages the site will need.

steps.name: Take the brand as tokens
steps.body: Color, type and spacing are lifted from the client's own material and written as design tokens, so the site looks like them and not like a template.

steps.name: Build it in Astro, Croatian first
steps.body: Static pages, Croatian as the primary language, English and any others alongside it, with hreflang and LocalBusiness JSON-LD in the markup.

steps.name: Audit it with Playwright
steps.body: An automated pass walks every page before anyone sees it, including a check that each image renders at the aspect ratio it was cropped for.

steps.name: Deploy to Cloudflare Pages
steps.body: The site goes live on Cloudflare's edge and the client gets a URL they can put straight in their Instagram bio.

pipeline.alsoBody: Velum's motion graphics were made in Remotion by the team that built the site — same brand tokens, same source material, rendered from code.

hero.label: Method
hero.title: Our method is a public repository. Read it.
hero.lead: We build software with orchestrated AI agents, and we wrote down the rules they run under. AGENTS.md, DESIGN.md, the 51 commands that run them, and the gate that stops their output from landing unread — all published under Apache-2.0.
hero.repoSummary: Four files in every repo, the schema they are versioned on, and 51 commands that run them.

howItWorks.label: How it works
howItWorks.title: Four moves, repeated until they are boring.
howItWorks.intro: The same four moves in every repository we touch, including yours. Nothing here depends on a person remembering how we do things.
artifacts: AGENTS.md — how agents work in this repo, and what they may not do.
DESIGN.md — tokens, type scale, component rules, and the do-not list.
The context snapshot — the current shape of the repo, generated and never hand-written.
The task ledger — tasks, sub-tasks, tags, and status, versioned next to the code.

steps.label: Every repository carries a versioned contract
steps.description: It sits on a schema with migrations. An agent starting work reads the same files a new engineer would.

steps.label: Work is split into scoped packets
steps.description: A packet names the files it may touch, the outcome it owes, and the check that proves it. Packets that do not overlap run at the same time on isolated workers.

steps.label: Every diff is read again by something that did not write it
steps.description: A worker finishes and stops. The orchestrator walks the change line by line and runs the checks against it. Work that fails goes back with the failure attached.

steps.label: A human owns the commit
steps.description: Commits are atomic and human-verified. Workers have no push access, so nothing reaches a branch that a person has not signed for.

rule.label: The operating rule
rule.rule: Agents propose; a human-verified gate commits. Workers never push.

clauses.detail: A worker produces a diff and a report. That is the whole of its authority.
The diff is re-read and the checks run before an atomic commit lands.
No worker holds push access. There is no path from agent output to your branch that skips a person.

why.label: What you get
why.title: Three things a public method buys you.
why.intro: You are not buying enthusiasm about agents. You are buying written rules.
why.noteP1: We operate on third-party agent runtimes and terminal tooling. We did not write them and do not claim them.
why.noteP2: What we built and open-sourced is what makes them repeatable: AGENTS.md and DESIGN.md on a versioned schema, the task ledger, and the packet format.

reasons.title: Throughput without unreviewed agent output
reasons.text: Several scoped packets run at once. None of them can commit. Speed comes from parallelism, not from skipping the read.

reasons.title: Context that lives in the repo, not in someone's chat history
reasons.text: AGENTS.md, DESIGN.md, and the task ledger are files in your codebase. Hand the project to another team and the knowledge goes with it.

reasons.title: A method you can audit
reasons.text: The contract schema, the command surface, and the gate are public. Read them before you sign anything.

company.label: The company
company.title: Two kinds of work, one set of checks.
company.p1: Client work usually starts the same way: something already runs, and the software around it has stopped explaining it. Nobody can see the current state, the operators keep a private spreadsheet, and the people who need to trust the output cannot check it.
company.p2: Voyager, Polis and Funda are not a side activity. They are where we hit the hard constraints first: fine-grained authorization, audit trails nobody can quietly rewrite, multilingual content that has to stay correct, deploys that have to keep working. We pay for those lessons on our own time and bring the result to client work.
company.p3: You can read how we work before you hire us: AGENTS.md, DESIGN.md, 51 commands, and the gate that puts a human in front of every commit. All of it is public under Apache-2.0.

content.title: Responsibility for content
content.body: {siteName} is responsible for the content published on {host}. We write it ourselves and keep it current to the best of our knowledge. Descriptions of our own software state what is live, what is a demonstration, and what is not built yet.

links.title: External links
links.body: This site links to pages operated by other people — repositories, client sites, third-party services. Their operators are responsible for what those pages contain. We check a link when we add it; we cannot check it continuously. Tell us at <mail>{email}</mail> if one is broken or wrong and we will remove or correct it.

copyright.title: Copyright
copyright.body: Text, images, and code published on this site belong to {siteName} unless another owner is named. Quote us with a source link. Ask before reproducing a page in full. Agent Ops Cockpit, the software we build with, is published separately under the Apache-2.0 licence, and that licence governs its use.

form.title: The contact form
form.body: The form on our <link>contact section</link> submits the name, email address, company, topic, and message you type. We store that submission and send it to ourselves by email so we can answer you. We do not use it for anything else and we do not sell it. Ask us to delete your message and we will.

ContactForm.messageLabel: What is hard to understand, slow to operate, or difficult to trust?
ContactForm.sentBody: It landed with us. The reply comes from {email}, within one working day.
ContactForm.fallbackFailed: We could not store the message just now.
ContactForm.fallbackMailClient: This form hands the message to your mail app.
ContactForm.fallbackTail: Your mail app should have opened with everything filled in. If it did not, send it to <mail>{email}</mail>.
ContactForm.errorEmail: We need an address we can reply to.
ContactForm.errorMessage: A sentence or two about the system is enough.
